items.prompt:
I tiptoed down the stairs, my heart thumping. Was anyone awake?

Who is telling this story?

options.text: a narrator outside the story who sees everything
options.why: The word I shows the narrator is a character, not an outsider.

options.text: the reader
options.why: The reader does not tell the story.

options.text: the character, using the word I
a different person each time
options.why: One voice, I, tells the whole passage.

hints: Look at the pronoun in the first sentence.
Who is I?
Is the speaker part of the story or watching from outside?
items.explanation: The word I shows a character is telling the story. This is first-person viewpoint.

items.prompt:
Leo tiptoed down the stairs. He wondered if anyone was awake.

From which viewpoint is this told?

options.text: third person, with a narrator outside the story
first person, as if Leo is speaking
options.why: First person uses I or we. This text says he.

options.text: second person, speaking to you
options.why: The text does not say you.

options.text: no one is telling it
options.why: Every story has a narrator.

hints: Look for I, we, you or he/she/they.
The text says Leo and he.
The narrator is outside the story.
items.explanation: The narrator uses Leo and he, so the story is told in the third person.

items.prompt: Which sentence is told in the first person?

options.text: The twins ran to the gate.
options.why: This is third person. The narrator talks about the twins.

options.text: She picked up the lost kitten.
options.why: This is third person. It uses she.

options.text: Bayu waved as the bus drove away.
options.why: This is third person. It uses Bayu.

options.text: We ran to the gate and I picked up the lost kitten.

hints: First person uses I, me, my, we or our.
Cross out sentences about other people by name.
Find the sentence with I or we.
items.explanation: We and I show that the narrator was there and is a character. That is first person.

items.prompt: Change this sentence to first person: Leo felt his hands shake.

options.text: He felt his hands shake.
options.why: This is still third person.

options.text: I felt my hands shake.
You felt your hands shake.
options.why: This is second person, not first.

options.text: Leo felt my hands shake.
options.why: The names and pronouns do not match.

hints: First person uses I and my.
Replace Leo with the narrator.
Change his to match.
items.explanation: In first person, Leo becomes I and his becomes my: I felt my hands shake.

items.prompt:
The attic was dim and dusty. A cobweb swayed in the draught, and the floorboards groaned.

Choose 3 words or phrases that show the attic has not been used for a long time.

options.text: dim and dusty
The attic
options.why: This only names the place. It does not describe it.

options.text: a cobweb
groaned

hints: Look for words that describe how the attic looks and sounds.
Dust and cobwebs build up when nobody cleans.
One option only names the place.
items.explanation: Dim, dusty, a cobweb and groaning floorboards all suggest an old place that no one visits. The phrase the attic just names it.

items.prompt: Joko wipes the board, feeds the class fish and picks up litter without being asked. What kind of person is Joko?

options.text: lazy
options.why: A lazy person would not do jobs without being asked.

options.text: helpful
angry
options.why: Nothing here shows anger.

options.text: shy
options.why: These actions do not tell us about shyness.

hints: Look at what Joko does.
He does these jobs without being asked.
What word describes someone who likes to help?
items.explanation: Joko does useful jobs without being told. His actions show he is helpful.

items.prompt: Match each planning tool to the job it does best.
pairs: plan the opening, problem and ending of a story
collect lots of ideas about one topic
put events in the order they happened
record facts about a person in your story
hints: Each tool is shaped to help with one job.
A timeline works with time.
A character profile is about a character.
items.explanation: A story mountain plans the plot, a spider diagram collects ideas, a timeline orders events and a character profile records details about a character.

items.prompt: Sort these details for a character profile.
hints: A profile has different sections.
Appearance is what you see.
Personality is what the character is like inside.
items.explanation: Appearance is how a character looks. Personality is the kind of person they are. Likes and dislikes are what they enjoy or avoid.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a story plan in order.
items: Opening: meet the characters and setting
Build-up: something starts to go wrong
hints: A story starts by showing who and where.
The most exciting moment comes after the build-up.
The ending comes last.
items.explanation: A story often begins with an opening, builds up to the problem, solves it and then ends.

items.prompt:
Amara packed her raincoat, her torch and a spare battery. The sky was already darkening, and the wind was growing stronger. She set off along the coast path.

What is most likely to happen next?

options.text: Amara will give up and go back to bed.
options.why: She has already set off, so this does not follow.

options.text: She will find a treasure on the first step.
options.why: The story gives no clue about treasure.

options.text: She will meet a talking fish.
options.why: The text gives no clue about a fantasy.

options.text: A storm will break while she is on the path.

hints: Look at the clues about the weather.
Amara has packed for rain and darkness.
What do darkening skies and strong winds often lead to?
items.explanation: The darkening sky, strong wind and raincoat suggest a storm. The clues in the text point to what happens next.

items.prompt:
Wulan had told everyone she could not swim. Now she stood by the pool, holding a tiny blue float. Behind her, her little brother leaned over the edge and began to slip.

What will probably happen next?

options.text: Wulan will throw the float to her brother and call for help.
Wulan will walk away without a word.
options.why: This does not fit her actions. She is holding a float.

options.text: Her brother will turn into a fish.
options.why: Nothing in the text suggests magic.

options.text: Wulan will start to sing.
options.why: Nothing in the text points to singing.

hints: Look at the object Wulan holds.
Her brother is in danger.
She cannot swim, so what could she do instead?
items.explanation: Wulan cannot swim, but she holds a float and sees her brother slipping. The most likely action is to throw the float and call for help.

items.prompt: In a story, Maya finds a lost kitten, takes it home and her mum says she can keep it. Which is an alternative ending that still fits the story?

options.text: Maya wins a prize in a maths test.
options.why: This ending is about a different part of Maya's life and does not fit.

options.text: Maya becomes a pilot and flies to the moon.
options.why: This ending does not fit a story about a kitten.

options.text: Maya finds the kitten's owner on the poster at the bus stop and returns it.
Maya adopts a hundred dragons.
options.why: This ending does not fit the story, which is not a fantasy.

hints: An alternative ending changes how the story finishes.
It must still make sense with the beginning.
Look for an ending that is still about the kitten.
items.explanation: The new ending changes what happens to the kitten, but it still fits the story about finding a lost animal.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows a character's own opinion about a setting?

options.text: The forest covered ten hectares of the island.
options.why: This is a fact about size, not an opinion.

options.text: A path ran through the forest to the lake.
options.why: This describes where the path is, not what a character thinks.

options.text: “I hate this forest,” grumbled Tom. “It is damp and gloomy.”
Pine trees grew on both sides.
options.why: This is a plain description of the trees.

hints: An opinion tells what someone thinks or feels.
Look for words like hate, love, damp and gloomy.
Whose voice do we hear in the sentence?
items.explanation: Tom says he hates the forest and calls it damp and gloomy. That is his own opinion of the setting.

items.prompt: A story is set in 1900. The characters write letters by hand, travel by horse cart and light their rooms with oil lamps. What does this tell the reader?

options.text: The story is set a long time ago.
The author did not know how to use a car.
options.why: The details are about the time of the story, not what the author knows.

options.text: The story takes place on another planet.
options.why: Nothing points to another planet.

options.text: The characters are not real people.
options.why: This detail does not show whether characters are real.

hints: Look at the tools and transport in the story.
Which of them would you see in a modern city?
Authors use details like these to show when a story takes place.
items.explanation: The old tools and transport show the time the story is set in. Fiction often shows how people lived at that time.

items.prompt:
Nia's voice was a whisper. She hid behind her mum and stared at her shoes.

Choose 3 details that show Nia is shy.

options.text: Her voice was a whisper.
She hid behind her mum.
She stared at her shoes.
Her mum was standing near the door.
options.why: This tells where Mum stood. It does not show how Nia feels.

hints: Look at what Nia says and does.
Which actions would a confident child avoid?
One detail only tells where Mum stood.
items.explanation: A whispering voice, hiding behind Mum and staring at her shoes all show shyness. Where Mum stands says nothing about how Nia feels.

items.prompt:
Version A: The dog barked at the postman and the postman jumped. Version B: I barked as loudly as I could. This human wore a funny hat and smelt of paper!

Which version lets us know what the narrator thinks and feels?

options.text: Version A, because it tells the whole event
options.why: Version A tells what happened but not what a character feels.

options.text: both versions equally
options.why: Only one version shares a narrator's own thoughts.

options.text: neither version
options.why: One version does show the narrator's feelings.

options.text: Version B, because the narrator describes the event in their own voice

hints: Look at who tells each version.
Which version uses I?
Which one shows opinions such as funny hat?
items.explanation: Version B is told by the dog as I, so we hear its thoughts. Version A is told from outside and only reports what happened.
